title: Composition of the Electoral Tribunals
ask: How is each Electoral Tribunal (SET and HRET) composed and organized under Art. VI, Secs. 17 and 19?
items: Each chamber has its own Electoral Tribunal: nine Members in all
Three Justices of the Supreme Court, designated by the Chief Justice
Six Members of the Senate or House, as the case may be
The six are chosen on proportional representation from political parties and registered party-list groups represented in the chamber
The senior Justice in the Tribunal is its Chairman (not someone the Chief Justice picks as chair)
Constituted within thirty days after the chamber organizes with the election of the Senate President and Speaker (Sec. 19)
src: Art. VI, Secs. 17 and 19

title: Nature of the Electoral Tribunals
ask: What is the nature of the Electoral Tribunals? Give the four features (including the three subjects of their jurisdiction).
items: Exclusive jurisdiction: ‘sole judge’ of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of their Members
Independent: jurisdiction shared neither with the chamber nor with the courts (Bondoc)
Non-partisan: a non-political body though two-thirds of its members are politicians
Not beyond review: the Supreme Court may correct grave abuse of discretion by certiorari (Abayon)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 17; Bondoc v. Pineda; Abayon v. HRET (2016); class reviewer

title: Valid grounds to end tribunal membership
ask: What are the five valid grounds for terminating a legislator’s membership in an Electoral Tribunal (Bondoc v. Pineda)? Party disloyalty is not one.
items: Expiration of the Member’s congressional term of office
Death or permanent disability
Resignation from the political party he represents in the tribunal
Formal affiliation with another political party
Removal for other valid cause
src: Bondoc v. Pineda (1991)

title: When HRET or SET jurisdiction attaches
ask: What three things must concur before the HRET (or SET) acquires jurisdiction over a winner, ending COMELEC’s (Reyes v. COMELEC)?
items: A valid proclamation
A proper oath of office: for the House, before the Speaker and in open session
Assumption of office (the term begins at noon of June 30)
src: Reyes v. COMELEC (2013); Lico v. COMELEC (party-list nominees)

title: When COMELEC keeps jurisdiction (no tribunal yet)
ask: In what situations does COMELEC keep jurisdiction, so the Electoral Tribunal has nothing to take over?
items: Proclamation, oath and assumption have not all concurred (Reyes v. COMELEC)
The validity of the proclamation itself is pending before COMELEC on a timely motion for reconsideration (Codilla)
The candidate’s COC was finally cancelled before the election, so there is no ‘Member’ to judge (Velasco)
The issue is review of a COMELEC ruling: the tribunal cannot review COMELEC resolutions (Codilla)
Registration or cancellation of a party-list group, even one with a sitting member (An Waray)
Party-list leadership and nomination disputes before the nominee assumes office (Lokin)
src: Reyes v. COMELEC; Codilla v. De Venecia; Velasco v. Speaker; An Waray; Lokin

title: Codilla and Velasco rules
ask: What rules do Codilla v. De Venecia and Velasco v. Speaker lay down on contested proclamations and House recognition?
items: A timely motion for reconsideration suspends a COMELEC Division’s ruling
A proclamation made without notice and hearing is void
While COMELEC’s ruling on the proclamation is not final, the HRET does not acquire jurisdiction
Codilla: votes for a candidate not disqualified by final judgment are not stray; the second placer cannot be proclaimed
Velasco: votes for a candidate whose COC was cancelled as void are stray; the qualified top vote-getter wins
Once the ruling is final, the Speaker’s oath and the Secretary-General’s Roll entry are ministerial: mandamus lies
src: Codilla v. De Venecia (2002); Velasco v. Speaker (2016)

title: Annulment of elections vs failure of elections
ask: Give five differences between the Electoral Tribunal’s annulment of election results and COMELEC’s declaration of a failure of elections (Abayon).
items: Body: annulment by the Electoral Tribunal; failure of elections declared by COMELEC
Nature: annulment is a judicial function; declaring a failure is administrative
Scope: annulment covers only precincts connected with the contest; failure covers the entire election in the precinct or unit
Purpose: annulment finds who got the majority of legal votes; failure aims to hold or continue the election
Grounds for failure: election not held, suspended, or resulted in a failure to elect
Aftermath: no special election after annulment; special elections follow a declaration of failure
src: Abayon v. HRET (2016); class reviewer table

title: Requisites for annulling election results
ask: When may an Electoral Tribunal annul election results, a drastic remedy (Abayon v. HRET)? Give the two requisites and the evidentiary rule.
items: Illegal ballots affect over 50% of votes cast in the precinct (for a unit, over 50% of its precincts and votes)
The lawful ballots cannot be distinguished from the unlawful ones with reasonable certainty
Findings of fraud, terrorism or other irregularities must rest on substantial evidence; otherwise grave abuse
src: Abayon v. HRET (2016)

title: Who must sit: inhibition and quorum rules
ask: What are the rules on disqualification, inhibition and quorum in the Electoral Tribunals (Abbas; Reyes v. HRET)?
items: Legislator-members cannot all be disqualified, even if the contest names all of them (Abbas)
The three Justices alone cannot decide; no rule amendment can give them that power (Abbas)
Individual members may inhibit as conscience dictates (Abbas)
A rule requiring at least one Justice for a quorum is valid; no equal protection violation (Reyes v. HRET)
Why valid: collegial body from two departments; Justices tone down politics; only a Justice can chair
If inhibitions break the quorum, the Supreme Court and the House may designate special members (Reyes v. HRET)
src: Abbas v. SET (1988); Reyes v. HRET (2018)

title: Composition of the Commission on Appointments
ask: What is the composition of the Commission on Appointments (Art. VI, Sec. 18)? Give the four elements.
items: The President of the Senate, as ex officio Chairman
Twelve Senators
Twelve Members of the House of Representatives
Each House elects its twelve on proportional representation from political parties and registered party-list groups represented therein
src: Art. VI, Sec. 18

title: Commission on Appointments: voting and operating rules
ask: What are the constitutional rules on how the Commission on Appointments votes, acts and meets (Art. VI, Secs. 18–19)?
items: The Chairman shall not vote, except in case of a tie
It shall act on all appointments within thirty session days of Congress from their submission
It shall rule by a majority vote of all the Members
Constituted within thirty days after both Houses organize with the election of the Senate President and Speaker
Meets only while Congress is in session
Meets at the call of its Chairman or a majority of all its Members
Its power is exercised by the CA as a body, not by individual members
src: Art. VI, Secs. 18 and 19; class reviewer

title: Appointments needing CA confirmation
ask: Which four categories of presidential appointments require the consent of the Commission on Appointments (Art. VII, Sec. 16)?
items: Heads of the executive departments
Ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls
Officers of the armed forces from the rank of colonel or naval captain
Other officers whose appointments are vested in the President by the Constitution (e.g., constitutional commissioners)
src: Art. VII, Sec. 16 (first sentence); class reviewer

title: Limits on the confirmation power
ask: What are the limits on the Commission on Appointments’ confirmation power?
items: Congress cannot by statute require CA confirmation for offices outside Art. VII, Sec. 16’s first sentence
Appointments made while Congress is not in session are effective until CA disapproval or the next adjournment of Congress
The Vice-President’s appointment to the Cabinet requires no confirmation (Art. VII, Sec. 3)
The CA’s rules of procedure are its own, outside the reach of Congress and the courts (class reviewer)
src: Art. VII, Secs. 3 and 16; class reviewer

title: Computing CA seats (proportional representation)
ask: How are seats in the Commission on Appointments computed, and what rules govern fractions and thresholds (Guingona; Coseteng)?
items: Senate: party’s seats = (party’s senators ÷ 24) × 12; House computed the same way on its total membership
The rule is mandatory: no discretion for the majority party (Guingona)
Fractions cannot be rounded up at another party’s expense (Guingona)
A party needs at least two senators for one seat; a lone senator’s 0.5 gets none (Guingona)
House: a party needs about one-twelfth of the membership (some 17 then) for one seat (Coseteng)
Minority status alone gives no seat; endorsements by members of other parties do not count (Coseteng)
The CA may function with fewer than 12 from a chamber, so long as it has a majority (Guingona)
Guingona numbers: LDP 15 senators = 7.5 (not 8); NPC 2.5; Lakas 1.5; LP-PDP 0.5 (none)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 18; Guingona v. Gonzales (1992); Coseteng v. Mitra (1990)

title: When a chamber may reshuffle its CA contingent
ask: When may a chamber change its members in the Commission on Appointments (Daza v. Singson)?
items: When political alignments in the chamber change, to keep proportional representation
The change must be permanent, not a temporary alliance or factional division
It must involve severance of political loyalties or formal disaffiliation (e.g., mass transfer to a new party)
The new party need not prove a track record or long existence to be counted
Contrast Bondoc: tribunal members cannot be removed for how they vote
src: Daza v. Singson (1989); Bondoc v. Pineda (1991)

title: Suing over tribunal or CA composition
ask: What rules govern a court challenge to the composition of an Electoral Tribunal or the Commission on Appointments?
items: Justiciable, not political: legality of the manner of filling seats is reviewable (Daza; Guingona)
Only each chamber elects its tribunal and CA members; the bodies cannot reconstitute themselves (Pimentel v. HRET)
Primary recourse is the chamber; the Court intervenes only if the chamber fails to comply (Pimentel; Drilon)
Standing: the petitioner must show that she or her party was deprived of a seat (Drilon)
Relief: prohibition voids the improper election to the CA (Guingona: Romulo and Tañada)
src: Daza; Guingona v. Gonzales; Pimentel v. HRET; Drilon v. De Venecia

title: Electoral Tribunal vs Commission on Appointments
ask: Contrast the Electoral Tribunals and the Commission on Appointments on composition, chair, function, number and meetings.
items: Composition: ET has 3 Justices + 6 legislators; CA has the Senate President + 12 Senators + 12 Representatives
Chair: ET’s senior Justice; CA’s Senate President, ex officio, voting only to break a tie
Function: ET is the sole judge of election contests (judicial); CA confirms appointments
Number: one ET per chamber; one CA for both Houses
Meetings: CA meets only while Congress is in session; no such limit for the ETs
Common: proportional representation of parties and party-list groups; constituted within 30 days (Sec. 19)
src: Art. VI, Secs. 17–19

title: Plenary legislative power
ask: What is the scope of Congress’s plenary legislative power, and what examples from the cases show it?
items: Vested in Congress (Senate and House), except as reserved to the people by initiative and referendum (Art. VI, Sec. 1)
Broad, general and comprehensive: for all purposes of civil government
Any power legislative by usage and tradition belongs to Congress unless the Constitution lodged it elsewhere
Limited only by the Constitution, expressly or impliedly
Example: creating municipalities and other local units (Torralba)
Example: creating legislative districts, hence provinces and cities, belongs only to Congress (Sema)
Example: fixing election schedules, subject to suffrage and due process (Macalintal, 2023)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 1; Torralba; Sema; Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023)

title: Sema v. COMELEC rules
ask: Why could the ARMM not create the province of Shariff Kabunsuan, and what did Sema leave intact?
items: Only Congress may create legislative districts (Art. VI, Sec. 5)
Creating a province or city creates a district, so only Congress may create them
The Constitution gives autonomous regions no such power (expressio unius est exclusio alterius)
An inferior body created by Congress cannot change Congress’s own membership
A regional assembly legislates only on regional matters within its territory
The ARMM may still create municipalities and barangays, which create no district
COMELEC Res. 7902 was valid: it merely kept the existing district
src: Sema v. COMELEC (2008)

title: Creating local government units (Torralba)
ask: What rules on the creation of local government units come from Torralba v. Sibagat?
items: Creating a municipal corporation is essentially a legislative power
Once a Local Government Code is enacted, creations must conform to its criteria
Before the Code exists, the power remains plenary, subject only to a plebiscite in the units affected
Sibagat was de jure: the plebiscite approved it and its officers took oaths and performed their duties
src: Torralba v. Municipality of Sibagat (1987)

title: Gatmaytan’s five substantive limits
ask: What are the five substantive limitations on legislative power in Gatmaytan’s book?
items: Unconstitutional laws: no law beyond Congress’s power or contrary to the Constitution
Supermajority votes: Congress cannot require a higher vote to amend or repeal a law
Irrepealable laws: no law can be placed beyond repeal by later Congresses
Retroactive laws: laws are prospective; no ex post facto laws or bills of attainder
The Supreme Court’s fiscal autonomy and rule-making power (e.g., no exemption from court fees)
src: Gatmaytan, P&S; Art. III, Sec. 22; Art. VIII, Secs. 3 and 5(5)

title: When a law is unconstitutional; partial nullity
ask: In what three ways can a law be unconstitutional, and what happens when only part of it is void?
items: It is beyond the legislature’s power to enact
It creates or establishes methods or forms that infringe constitutional principles
Its purpose or effect violates the Constitution or its basic principles
Laws are presumed constitutional; courts strike them down only on a clear breach
Partial nullity: valid parts stand unless so dependent on the void parts that the legislature meant them as a whole
src: Gatmaytan, P&S; class reviewer; ABAKADA (separability); Lidasan (inseparable)

title: Class reviewer’s other limits on legislation
ask: Besides Gatmaytan’s five, what other limitations on legislative power does the class reviewer list (eight)?
items: Riders: Sec. 25(2) for the budget; Sec. 26(1) for bills generally
One subject, expressed in the title (Sec. 26(1))
No amendment on third reading (Sec. 26(2)), though the bicameral conference may reconcile versions
Uniform and equitable, progressive taxation (Sec. 28(1))
No increase in the Supreme Court’s appellate jurisdiction without its advice and concurrence (Sec. 30)
No legislative veto (ABAKADA)
No delegation of legislative power, except permitted delegations
Sunset clauses: a law may fix a date after which it ceases to be effective
src: Art. VI, Secs. 25(2), 26, 28(1), 30; class reviewer

title: Other express limits on Congress
ask: Name five other express constitutional limits on what Congress may legislate (rule map list).
items: The Bill of Rights
No adding qualifications to offices whose qualifications the Constitution fixes (SJS v. DDB)
No titles of royalty or nobility (Art. VI, Sec. 31)
No interpreting the Constitution by statute (Endencia v. David)
The money provisions (Art. VI, Secs. 24 to 29)
src: Art. III; Art. VI, Secs. 24–29, 31; SJS v. DDB; Endencia v. David

title: Three forms of congressional oversight (ABAKADA)
ask: What are the three categories of congressional oversight in ABAKADA, and which survive enactment?
items: Scrutiny: lesser intensity; reports and information, budget hearings, question hour, confirmation of appointments
Investigation: a more intense digging of facts, through inquiries in aid of legislation
Supervision: a continuing and informed awareness of executive operations
Only scrutiny and investigation survive enactment; supervision with a right to approve rules is a legislative veto
src: ABAKADA Guro v. Purisima (2008)

title: Why a legislative veto is void
ask: Why is a post-enactment congressional approval power (legislative veto) unconstitutional, and which cases applied this?
items: Separation of powers: Congress takes part in executing the law
Bicameralism: a committee or one House acts for the whole Congress
Presentment: Congress acts with the force of law without submitting a bill to the President
ABAKADA: JCOC approving RA 9335’s IRR void; the rest saved by the separability clause
Macalintal (2003): JCOC approving COMELEC rules void; it also violates COMELEC’s independence
Belgica (2013): legislators’ post-enactment identification and realignment of PDAF projects void
src: ABAKADA (2008); Macalintal v. COMELEC (2003); Belgica (2013)

title: Is the oversight committee valid?
ask: Which oversight committee powers are valid and which are invalid? (2023 midterm: Tax Code Sec. 290-A)
items: Valid: review and monitor implementation
Valid: require reports and information from agencies
Valid: hold hearings and recommend remedial legislation
Invalid: approve or disapprove rules, IRRs, agency budgets or projects
Invalid: deputize or direct executive agencies (e.g., BIR, BOC, PNP, NBI), or otherwise enforce the law
Remedy: void only the offending clause and save the rest if separable
‘In aid of legislation’ cannot cure an executive role
src: ABAKADA; Art. VII, Sec. 17; 2023 midterm Q3

title: The non-delegation principle
ask: State the non-delegation principle and its three propositions.
items: Potestas delegata non delegari potest: what has been delegated cannot be delegated
The delegated power is a duty the delegate must perform by its own judgment, not through another’s mind
Congress cannot delegate the power to make the law (what it shall be), but may confer discretion in its execution
No subdelegation to private parties: the LTFRB could not let operators set their own fares (KMU)
src: Class reviewer (separation of powers); rule map; KMU v. Garcia

title: Tests of valid delegation
ask: What two tests must a delegation of legislative power pass?
items: Completeness: the law sets forth the policy to be executed, leaving the delegate only to carry it out
Sufficient standard: the law fixes limits, sufficiently determinate or determinable, to which the delegate must conform
src: Rule map; class reviewer; Zabal dissent
hook: Complete policy plus fence: the policy says where to go, the standard says how far

title: Permissible delegations of legislative power
ask: What are the five permissible delegations of legislative power?
items: Tariff powers to the President (Art. VI, Sec. 28(2))
Emergency powers to the President (Art. VI, Sec. 23(2))
To the people at large: initiative and referendum (Art. VI, Sec. 32; RA 6735)
To local governments
To administrative bodies: subordinate (supplementary and contingent) rule-making
src: Art. VI, Secs. 23(2), 28(2), 32; class reviewer
hook: PLATE: People, Local governments, Administrative bodies, Tariff, Emergency

title: Delegation cases: valid and undue
ask: Classify the delegation cases in coverage as valid or undue, with the reason.
items: Undue: People v. Vera, provincial boards decide whether the Probation Act applies (no standard)
Undue: KMU, LTFRB lets bus operators set their own fares (subdelegation to private parties)
Undue: John Hay, proclamation extends Subic tax incentives without statutory authority
Valid: Agustin v. Edu, LOI and rules on early warning devices (sufficient standard)
Valid: Garcia, tariff EOs under ‘national economy, general welfare and/or national security’
Valid: Zabal, Boracay closure proclamation (dissent: no statute delegated the power)
src: Vera; KMU; John Hay PAC v. Lim; Agustin; Garcia v. Exec. Sec.; Zabal

title: Requisites of emergency powers (Sec. 23(2))
ask: What conditions does Art. VI, Sec. 23(2) impose on delegating emergency powers to the President?
items: There must be war or other national emergency
Congress must act by law
The delegation is for a limited period only
It is subject to such restrictions as Congress may prescribe
The powers must be necessary and proper to carry out a declared national policy
Unless sooner withdrawn by resolution of Congress, they cease upon its next adjournment
src: Art. VI, Sec. 23(2)

title: Requisites of a valid IRR
ask: What are the four requisites of a valid implementing rule or regulation (Gatmaytan, citing Lokin)?
items: Its promulgation is authorized by the legislature
It is within the scope of the authority given
It is promulgated in accordance with the prescribed procedure
It is reasonable: germane to the law and consistent with its standards
Corollary: an IRR cannot amend, expand or contradict the law it implements
src: Gatmaytan’s book, citing Lokin v. COMELEC (2010)

title: What must be published (Tañada)
ask: Under Tañada v. Tuvera, what must be published before it takes effect?
items: All statutes, including those of local application and private laws
Presidential decrees and executive issuances made in the exercise of legislative power
Administrative rules that enforce or implement existing law under a valid delegation (IRRs)
Publication must be in full, in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation
src: Tañada v. Tuvera (1985 and 1986); EO 200

title: What need not be published
ask: What three kinds of issuances need not be published under Tañada v. Tuvera?
items: Interpretative rules and regulations
Purely internal rules regulating only the agency’s personnel, not the public
Letters of instruction from administrative superiors to subordinates on performing their duties
src: Tañada v. Tuvera (1986 resolution)

title: Effectivity of laws and agency rules
ask: What are the rules on when laws and agency rules take effect?
items: Laws take effect fifteen days after publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation (EO 200)
‘Unless otherwise provided’ lets the law change the date, never dispense with publication (Tañada)
Agencies must file three certified copies of each rule with the UP Law Center (ONAR) (Adm. Code, Book VII)
Agency rules take effect fifteen days after filing, unless a different date is fixed
Publication alone is not enough for agency rules: unfiled rules do not bind the public
src: Civil Code, Art. 2 as amended by EO 200; Tañada v. Tuvera; Administrative Code of 1987, Book VII, Secs. 3–4

title: Checklist for an IRR provision (2024 midterm)
ask: Run the five-point checklist on a law directing an agency to issue an IRR (2024 Bulacan Freeport Act question).
items: No legislative veto: Congress keeps no approval role after enactment (ABAKADA)
Consulting a private party is not delegating rule-making to it, but the agency must not let it dictate (KMU)
A deadline for issuing the IRR is directory; a late IRR is not void
Publication in a newspaper of general circulation suffices (Tañada; EO 200), but the IRR must also be filed with ONAR
The law itself must supply policy and standards (completeness and sufficient standard)
src: 2024 midterm Q3; ABAKADA; KMU; Tañada; Administrative Code, Book VII

title: Purposes of the one subject–one title rule
ask: What are the purposes of the rule that every bill embrace only one subject expressed in its title (Art. VI, Sec. 26(1))?
items: To prevent hodgepodge or log-rolling legislation (no conglomeration of unrelated subjects)
To prevent surprise or fraud on the legislature through provisions the title does not disclose
To fairly apprise the people of the subjects of legislation, so they may be heard on them
src: Art. VI, Sec. 26(1); Lidasan v. COMELEC (dual limitations); class reviewer on riders

title: When a title is defective
ask: When is a bill’s title defective, and with what consequence (Lidasan)?
items: It is misleading
It is too restrictive (narrower than the body)
It fails to reflect essential matters embraced in the law
Consequence: the provision is void; the whole law falls if the parts are inseparable (Lidasan)
src: Lidasan v. COMELEC (1967)

title: When the title rule is satisfied
ask: When does a law comply with the one subject–one title rule, and what corollaries apply (Giron; Cruz v. Paras)?
items: The title is comprehensive enough to include the general object of the law
All provisions are germane: not foreign to the subject, and means of carrying it out
The title need not be a complete index or catalogue of the contents
The rule is construed liberally, so as not to cripple legislation (Giron)
A title limits how far the law can be read: ‘regulate’ does not authorize ‘prohibit’ (Cruz v. Paras)
A longer title cannot cure a defect in the short title (class reviewer, Bayanihan Act)
src: Giron v. COMELEC (2013); Cruz v. Paras (1983); Lidasan; class reviewer Q&A

title: Passage requirements: Art. VI, Sec. 26(2)
ask: What does Art. VI, Sec. 26(2) require before a bill passed by either House can become a law, and what is the exception?
items: Three readings on separate days
Printed copies in final form distributed to the Members three days before passage
Exception: the President certifies the necessity of immediate enactment to meet a public calamity or emergency
Certification dispenses with both separate-day readings and the three-day printing (Tolentino)
On the last reading, no amendment is allowed
The vote is taken immediately, and the yeas and nays are entered in the Journal
src: Art. VI, Sec. 26(2); Tolentino v. Secretary of Finance (1994)

title: Bicameral conference committee rules
ask: What may a bicameral conference committee do, and what limits apply (Tolentino)?
items: It reconciles differing versions passed by the two Houses
The no-amendment-on-third-reading rule does not bar its changes
It may adopt either version, merge them, or add provisions found in neither
New provisions must be germane to the subject of the bill
Its report must be approved by both Houses before the bill goes to the President
src: Tolentino v. Secretary of Finance (1994); Art. VI, Sec. 26(2)

title: How a bill becomes a law
ask: List the steps by which a bill becomes a law, in order.
items: Filing; first reading of number, title and author; referral to committee
Committee hearings and committee report
Second reading: debate and amendments
Third reading: printed copies three days before; no amendments; vote by yeas and nays
Transmittal to the other House, which passes it through its own three readings
If versions differ: bicameral conference committee; report approved by both Houses
Enrolled bill signed by the Speaker and Senate President, certified by the Secretaries
Presentment: the President signs, vetoes, or lets thirty days lapse
Publication; effectivity fifteen days after unless the law provides otherwise
src: Art. VI, Secs. 26–27; House and Senate Rules; EO 200

title: Three ways a bill becomes law
ask: In what three ways does a bill passed by Congress become a law (Art. VI, Sec. 27(1))?
items: The President approves and signs it
Congress overrides his veto by two-thirds of all the Members of each House
The President does not communicate a veto within thirty days after receipt: it becomes law as if signed
src: Art. VI, Sec. 27(1)

title: Veto and override procedure
ask: What is the procedure after the President vetoes a bill (Art. VI, Sec. 27(1))?
items: The President returns the bill with his objections to the House where it originated
That House enters the objections at large in its Journal and reconsiders the bill
Two-thirds of all the Members of that House must agree to pass it
It goes, with the objections, to the other House, which also needs two-thirds of all its Members
Votes are by yeas or nays; names of Members voting for or against are entered in the Journal
The veto must be communicated within thirty days after the date of receipt
src: Art. VI, Sec. 27(1)

title: Numbers: tribunals, CA, bills and effectivity
ask: Give the numbers and thresholds for the Electoral Tribunals, the Commission on Appointments, bills, vetoes and effectivity.
items: Electoral Tribunal: nine Members (3 Justices, 6 legislators)
CA: Senate President + 12 Senators + 12 Representatives; acts within thirty session days; majority of all the Members
ET and CA constituted within thirty days after each House organizes
Bills: three readings on separate days; printed copies three days before passage, unless certified urgent
Veto: communicated within thirty days after receipt; override by two-thirds of all the Members of each House
Laws: effective fifteen days after publication, unless the law provides otherwise
Agency rules: effective fifteen days after filing with ONAR, unless a different date is fixed
src: Art. VI, Secs. 17–19, 26(2), 27(1); EO 200; Administrative Code, Book VII
